endings.text: Richardson never saw any of this. About three weeks before he died in April 1886, too ill to leave his bedroom, he marked on the drawings where the lights would go and told Glessner: 'There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished.' Digging began that June, and George and Frances threw the first soil. Glessner was convinced it was the house Richardson would most have liked to live in himself.

evidence.text: Richardson died before construction began, so he never saw the house built.

The front door is heavily paneled oak with iron straps and a large square window behind an iron grille.
Richardson would not have the front door's grille and the outside ironwork painted; it was Bower-Barffed, a process Glessner did not recall seeing elsewhere, which kept it from rust.

The 1958 landmark plaque praised the plan 'which opens the family rooms to the quiet serenity of an inner yard'.

Yellow glass under chipped white glass in the door leading to the courtyard gives the hall a feeling of sunlight even in cloudy weather.
The Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls was carried from the old house; one vine fifty-five feet long was replanted and trained its full length, and it flourished.
The courtyard walls are common brick of a slightly pinkish colour with grey limestone trim, and by special arrangement the same brick was used in the adjoining house.

opening.text: WALK: THE GLESSNER HOUSE. Summer 1904, 1800 Prairie Avenue. Ten stops on foot, all the way round one house: the corner, the Eighteenth Street side, the alley, the front door, the carriage passage and the courtyard inside. The story is mostly the owner's own, from the account he wrote for his children in 1923. Exteriors only; who is home today is not claimed.

premise: Walk all the way round Richardson's last house in summer 1904, from the street that stared at it to the sunny courtyard it hid, in ten stops on foot.

stops.text: An old Chicago saying called Prairie Avenue 'the sunny street that holds the sifted few'. Pullman's mansion stands diagonally across the corner, Kimball's French chateau across the avenue. Then there is this one: rough granite, small deep windows, steep red roofs. It was the last house Henry Hobson Richardson designed, and he never saw it built.

This is the side people talked about when the house was new. Passers-by remarked on the narrow windows, 'just enough to light the narrow corridors'. Richardson held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of': people only shroud them in shades and curtains. The house keeps its back to the street.

The great arch is the back door: a small corridor through it leads to the kitchen. It is also how the orchestra sneaks in. On New Year's Day 1903 a double quartet of horns slipped in by the Eighteenth Street door and up the back stairs, and at four o'clock began to play in the upper hall.

The west wing is the stable and carriage house, with its wide carriage doorway onto Eighteenth Street. Inside, its walls are white glazed brick. The furnace room is underneath it, so the dust, dirt and noise of coal and ashes never come into the house itself.

Round the corner, these gates in the alley open into the courtyard, and they let the Glessners pull off a trick. On 1 December 1887 the family moved everything in through here, 'before our neighbors suspected even that we were about to move'. That night they lit the new hearth with live fire carried from the old one.

The front door: heavy oak strapped with iron, a square window behind an iron grille. Richardson would not have the ironwork painted; it was Bower-Barffed against rust, a process Glessner never saw anywhere else. The wall looks like solid rock, but it is brick faced with granite slabs, with deep stones at every opening to keep up the illusion.

Not every visitor uses the front door. Here a carriage could leave Prairie Avenue and roll right under the house, through two paneled oak doors hung on heavy iron straps, and out into a private courtyard. Follow it through.

Inside, the house changes its mind. From the street it looked shut tight; here it opens up. Richardson put generous windows on this sunny courtyard side, letting in, Glessner wrote, 'a flood of sunlight when the sun shines in Chicago'. The family rooms look in on this quiet yard, not out at the street.

The rounded bay above the terrace steps is the entrance hall. Its door to this courtyard is glazed with yellow glass under chipped white glass, so the hall feels sunny even on grey days. The vines here came from the family's old house; one was fifty-five feet long and replanted whole. It flourished.

Behind these walls, 1904 is a busy year. Frances Glessner, who has kept a journal since 1879, has set up a silversmith's bench in the basement. Every winter and spring her Monday Morning Reading Class meets in the library. Years ago her son George's friends ran a telegraph company from his school room, wired to seven houses.

title: Meet the Glessner House
